title: Socialism and Marxism

cards.h: The ideology of the many who work
cards.b:
Socialism arose as a protest against the misery and inequality of early industrial capitalism. It dreams of a society based on cooperation and shared ownership, not private profit.

Within it, Marxism is the most powerful and most-asked branch. Marx's theory shaped revolutions in Russia (1917), China (1949), Cuba and elsewhere, and still shapes academic debate.

The syllabus asks you to understand the family of socialisms: utopian, Marxist, Leninist, revisionist and democratic socialism. You also need to explain why the USSR collapsed (1991) and what remains of socialism today. The India link is strong: Nehruvian socialism, the Preamble and the Directive Principles.

• Community: humans are social beings, and their nature is shaped by relationships.
  • Cooperation over competition.
  • Equality, especially of outcome and condition. Socialists want to reduce class divisions.
  • Need: goods should be shared according to need, not only merit or market value.
  • Common ownership: the main means of production (land, factories, banks) should be owned in common, by the state, cooperatives or the community.

They split over means (revolution or reform) and ends (full communism or a regulated market with a strong welfare state).

Heywood groups them as fundamentalist (abolish capitalism) and revisionist (reform it).

The word "socialism" appeared in the 1820s-30s. Early thinkers imagined model communities.

  • Robert Owen (1771-1858), mill owner, built the New Lanark model and the New Harmony community in the USA. He urged cooperative villages.
  • Charles Fourier (1772-1837), French thinker who planned communities called phalansteries.
  • Henri de Saint-Simon (1760-1825), who wanted society run by scientists and industrialists.

Marx and Engels called them utopian: they appealed to reason and goodwill but had no theory of class struggle or of how change would occur. Their own approach, they said, was scientific socialism.

Karl Marx (1818-83) and Friedrich Engels (1820-95) wrote The Communist Manifesto (1848). Marx's later masterwork is Capital, Volume 1 (1867).

Historical materialism: the way a society produces its material needs (the base) shapes its laws, politics and ideas (the superstructure). History moves through stages, each driven by conflict between classes: ancient slavery, feudalism, capitalism, then socialism and communism. The Manifesto begins: the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.

Details are in the Western thought lesson on Marx (0-9-6).

cards.h: Marx on capitalism and the end goal
cards.b:
• Surplus value: workers produce more value than they are paid for, and capitalists keep the difference. This is exploitation.
  • Alienation: under capitalism, workers are cut off from their product, their work, other people and their human nature (Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts, 1844).
  • Crises: competition, falling profit rates and overproduction create recurring crises. The working class (proletariat) grows and becomes conscious.
  • Revolution: the proletariat takes power. A transitional dictatorship of the proletariat follows (Critique of the Gotha Programme, 1875).
  • Communism: a classless, stateless society that works on the principle "from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs".

V.I. Lenin (1870-1924) adapted Marxism to a backward, peasant country.

  • What Is To Be Done? (1902): workers alone reach only trade-union consciousness. A disciplined vanguard party of professional revolutionaries must lead. The party's rule of open debate but binding decisions was later formalised as democratic centralism (1905-06).
  • Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism (1916): capitalism survives by exporting capital to colonies. War among powers is a result.
  • The State and Revolution (1917): the bourgeois state must be smashed, not taken over.

The Bolshevik seizure of power came in October 1917. Stalin then built "socialism in one country", with forced collectivisation and heavy state control. Trotsky argued for permanent world revolution. Mao relied on the peasantry (China, 1949).

Eduard Bernstein, Evolutionary Socialism (1899)

The revisionist. Capitalism was not collapsing, the middle class was not disappearing, and workers had the vote. So socialism should be won by gradual reform and democracy. Kautsky and Luxemburg opposed him.

The Fabians (founded 1884)

Sidney and Beatrice Webb, G.B. Shaw. Gradual, educative change through Parliament. The Labour Party grew from this tradition.

Social democracy after 1945

Anthony Crosland, The Future of Socialism (1956): the goal is equality, achieved through growth and welfare, not nationalising everything. In the 1990s, Anthony Giddens's The Third Way (1998) shaped Blair's New Labour, accepting markets.

cards.h: Critiques and the crisis of socialism
cards.b:
• Economic: Hayek and von Mises argued central planning cannot handle information ("calculation problem"). Shortages and low innovation hit the USSR and East Europe.
  • Political: one-party rule, repression and the gulag. Liberals say socialism ignores individual freedom.
  • Theoretical: Marx underrated nationalism, religion and the staying power of capitalism. Class is no longer the only identity (feminists, race, ecology).
  • Collapse: the Berlin Wall fell in 1989 and the USSR dissolved in December 1991. Fukuyama's "end of history" thesis followed.

Responses: market socialism (John Roemer), China's "socialism with Chinese characteristics" (market reforms from 1978), and a revival of social democracy and ecological socialism.

cards.h: Socialism in India: from the CSP to the Constitution
cards.b:
• Before 1947: Congress Socialist Party (1934) with Jayaprakash Narayan, Acharya Narendra Dev, Ram Manohar Lohia. The Communist Party of India was founded in 1925 (Kanpur). M.N. Roy was among the early Marxists. Bhagat Singh also read socialism.
  • Nehru: Congress's Avadi session (1955) resolved on a "socialistic pattern of society". The Planning Commission (1950), public-sector industry and mixed economy followed.
  • Constitution: Directive Principles, Articles 38 and 39 (equitable distribution, no concentration of wealth). The 42nd Amendment (1976) added "socialist" to the Preamble. On 25 November 2024 the Supreme Court dismissed petitions seeking its removal (Balram Singh v Union of India), saying Parliament's amending power extends to the Preamble.

cards.h: Socialism in India: Gandhi, Ambedkar and the Left
cards.b:
• Gandhi and Ambedkar: Gandhi's trusteeship; Ambedkar's state socialism (States and Minorities, 1947).
  • Left politics: Kerala elected one of the world's first communist governments through the ballot in 1957, under E.M.S. Namboodiripad. The Naxalbari uprising began in 1967.
  • Congress Socialist Party (1934) brought Acharya Narendra Dev, Jayaprakash Narayan and Ram Manohar Lohia together inside Congress.
  • The Avadi session (1955) adopted a "socialistic pattern of society" as the goal.
  • The 42nd Amendment (1976) added the word "socialist" to the Preamble.

"Marxism is dead, but Marx lives." Comment.
Distinguish between scientific and utopian socialism.
Examine Lenin's contribution to Marxism.
Discuss the evolution of social democracy. How does it differ from Marxism?

Structure: define socialism and its strands. Move from utopian to scientific. Explain the Marxist method and critique of capitalism briefly, then Lenin and the revisionist split. Cover the 1991 crisis and survival strategies. Add India: Nehru, Articles 38-39, the Preamble and Kerala. A comparison table of Marx, Lenin and Bernstein helps.
